- [T-2059] **CLOSED 2026-10-04 (agent `scrollclaim`) — the tasks page stopped scrolling whenever a drag opened sideways, and no SwiftUI gesture priority could have fixed it: a `DragGesture` on a row cannot hand a touch back to the enclosing `ScrollView` once it has one.** The owner: *"when im on ios, scrolling in the tasks page sometimes doesnt work."* **Reproduced on `Cadence-iPhone15` before anything was changed**, by injecting two drags that differ in nothing but their first three samples. A 168pt drag straight up a task row scrolled the page 157pt. The same drag, from the same point, opening with **14pt of sideways travel** and then running the same 168pt up, scrolled the page **zero** — the screenshots are byte-identical but for the clock. That is the whole of "sometimes": whether the opening points of a thumb's arc happen to be straight. **The cause is this row's own gesture, proved by mutation, twice.** With `.highPriorityGesture(dragGesture, including: .none)` the failing path scrolled; with `including: .subviews` — which disables only the drag and leaves every descendant gesture alive, removing the confound in the first mutation — it scrolled again. **Three candidate fixes were refuted by their own builds, not by argument.** `minimumDistance: 30` stayed dead. `.simultaneousGesture` stayed dead. Claiming the drag *vertical* and returning early out of `onChanged` stayed dead — a drag opening `(4, -13)`, which the old code reads as vertical on its first event, still scrolled nothing. So the file's own comment was **wrong where it mattered**: "It does not contest the enclosing `ScrollView`/`List` pan — that is a separate arbitration" is false, the arbitration is not separate, and the row wins it for any touch whose opening movement is not dead vertical. **The fix is to stop asking SwiftUI to do the one thing it has no word for.** `iOSRowHorizontalPanRecognizer` is a `UIGestureRecognizer` that goes to `.failed` **while it is still `.possible`** when the drag is not horizontal: a recognizer that fails before it begins never asks the scroll view's pan to stand down, so a declined drag scrolls as if the row carried no gesture at all. The decision itself lives in `CadenceSwipeActionSupport.axisClaim`, outside `#if os(iOS)` and therefore pinned by the macOS-built test target, and it reads the axis at a new `CadenceSwipeActionMetrics.claimDistance` of **24pt rather than 12** — measured, not chosen: the reported drag reads *horizontal* at 12 and *vertical* by 24, and a deliberate swipe travels 76pt to open a single action, so waiting for 24 costs it nothing. **The four invariants were each re-measured on the built app, not argued:** vertical scrolling works from a row and from the completion circle; a swipe opens the tray, a tap on an open row closes it, and a 260pt swipe commits the full swipe; a tap on the circle completes, a tap on the row opens Edit Task, and a tap on the estimate chip still opens its popover; and a 163pt swipe begun **on the completion circle** completes nothing. **One regression was found and fixed inside this ticket, and it is the same shape as the bug this container was built to close.** With the recognizer merely added, an identical 260pt swipe committed from the row's text and was *ignored* from the "45m" estimate chip — which sits at the trailing edge, exactly where a right-to-left swipe starts. Letting the two recognize simultaneously fixed that and re-opened the old bug: the swipe opened the tray **and** the chip's popover. The delegate therefore makes the row's controls *wait* for this recognizer (`shouldBeRequiredToFailBy`) and exempts pans, so the scroll view is never made to wait; on a tap there is no movement, the recognizer fails at touch-up, and the control fires as it always did. **The `DragClaim` enum and the `claim` state are gone**, and with them the stale-claim hazard that motivated this investigation: there is no longer a latch to go stale, because the axis is decided per touch by a recognizer UIKit resets itself. **KNOWN, not fixed here:** a vertical drag *begun on the completion circle* scrolls, but measurably less far than the same drag begun on the row's text (≈14pt against ≈67pt for a 152pt finger travel, from downsampled screenshots, so treat the numbers as ordinal). It is an improvement on scrolling nothing, and the cause was not chased. **NOT verified:** iPad, `List`-hosted rows, VoiceOver, Dynamic Type, and real-finger behaviour on hardware — every measurement here is injected touch samples on one simulator, and a real touch stream is smoothed in ways an injected one is not, so the *frequency* the owner experiences may differ from the sharp boundary measured here even though the mechanism does not.

An unreliable trigger is free only when its action is idempotent *upward*; this one is not, and 'no worse off than now' is false for a pass that removes. **The hazard is concrete, and today's own audit is what makes it so.** A pending `UNNotificationRequest` lives in the OS and survives a store replacement, and [[T-3042]]/[[T-3045]] (filed the same day) establish that a failed startup backup drops the launch into an **empty recovery store**. Later passes re-add them, because the diff converges, but nothing bounds how long 'later' is: an import stalled on a dropped network or a signed-out account leaves the queue swept with no trigger left to repair it. Whether `NSPersistentCloudKitContainer` posts one finished `.import` per sync or one per batch is a platform fact **not in this tree**, and [[T-2010]] already records that even *delivery* is unestablished without a two-device run. (3) The earlier store folders are a **separate** decision from the recovery one: they are outside the app's current container, `migrateLegacyStoreIfNeeded` still reads them, and deleting them would make the migration's own fallback unreachable. The row that shows all of them today carries `directory` and `onReveal` and nothing else, on purpose — whatever this ticket decides, the delete does not belong on that row. - [T-1783] **CLOSED 2026-09-30 (coordinator) — a sibling's commit silently REVERTS ledger prose written early, leaving `git status` clean and nothing in the declined-hunk ledger, and the rule that prevents it was written as sequencing advice.** Reported 2026-09-30 by agent `rawexcerpt` while closing [[T-1700]]: it wrote its closures early, a sibling committed `docs/TODO.md`, and its text was **simply gone** — working tree clean, original content restored, **no declined-hunk record**. Rewriting immediately before `agent-commit.sh` worked. **Why this is worse than [[T-679]] as documented:** T-679 is written up as "the index is shared, so commit through the script", and the commit-time rule reads like ordering hygiene. It is not. Whole-file staging means a sibling's commit of that path **overwrites your working-tree edit with HEAD's content and announces nothing** — the declined-hunk ledger records hunks a commit *refused*, not prose a checkout *lost*, so the one instrument that would report it is structurally blind here. An agent that wrote its ledger line an hour early and did not re-read it before committing would land a commit whose message describes work the ledger does not record, and every existing guard would pass. **The fix is documentation, deliberately**: `AGENTS.md` now states the mechanism and the absence of a signal, not just the instruction, in five lines inside its 200-line budget (192 → 197). **Not fixed in code, and the reason is the tradeoff:** the candidate fixes are a per-agent ledger fragment directory folded at commit, or teaching `agent-commit.sh` to diff the working tree against its last-seen copy — the first changes how every agent writes an entry, the second needs per-agent state the script deliberately does not keep. Neither is worth doing before the failure is seen a second time; it has been seen once, by an agent careful enough to notice its own prose had vanished. [[T-679]] [[T-974]] [[T-1385]]

But `claim` walks `booted_udids()`, which is `xcrun simctl list devices booted` in simctl's own order, and takes the first device it can `mkdir` a claim for. Note that `status` already prints the device as `free`, which is the same claim in the other direction. Until both land, the script's header and the script disagree, and the header is the half that is right.

That is the identical mistake to the bug itself, testing the documented intent instead of the allocation. Rewritten so the fixture lists a second fake **first**, standing in for the owner's device, via a `CADENCE_SIM_DENY_EXTRA` hook that is **additive only** — one that could remove an entry would be a way to hand out the owner's device by setting an environment variable. Both polarities asserted; re-mutated and **killed**, the failure naming the denied udid it wrongly allocated. Selftest 5 properties / 0 failures, live `claim` now answers `Cadence-iPhone15`. Thank you for filing it rather than working around it.

Its replacement, `maximumSideShareOfTheShorterSide = 0.5`, is live and is now the thing that sets the floor: a region examined whose shorter side is under 104px cannot hold a 52px square and be called a *corner*. - [T-1491] **CLOSED 2026-09-28 (agent `filedrop`) — the editor overrode `draggingEntered` and not `draggingUpdated`, so at a host that ACCEPTS images a dragged bitmap got Cadence's copy badge for one frame and AppKit's refusal for the rest of the drag.** Found while measuring [[T-1447]], which is refused above; this is the defect that measurement turned up instead. **The shape.** AppKit calls `draggingEntered` once, as the pointer crosses into the view, and `draggingUpdated` on every movement after that — so `draggingUpdated` is what draws the badge for all but the first frame, and what AppKit reads before it offers `performDragOperation` at all. [[T-478]], [[T-504]], [[T-511]] and [[T-1418]] all reasoned about `draggingEntered` alone and nothing in the app has ever overridden the other one (`rg draggingUpdated Cadence/` → zero hits before this commit). **Measured 2026-09-28, Xcode 27, one windowed `CadenceTextView` after AppKit's own `updateDragTypeRegistration`, one TIFF-only board, `MarkdownDropInfo` driving both calls:** at `allowsMarkdownImageInsertion == true`, `draggingEntered` → **`.copy`** (Cadence's rule) and `draggingUpdated` → **`[]`** (`super`, which refuses a bitmap because `importsGraphics` is off and must stay off — [[T-1418]], `nothingInTheAppTurnsOnImportsGraphics`). Calling `draggingEntered` a second time gave `.copy` again, so the two answers differ by which method was asked and by nothing else. At `allowsMarkdownImageInsertion == false` both gave `[]`, which is why this never showed at a refusing host and why four tickets could pass over it. **It is [[T-478]] with the sign reversed**: that ticket removed a copy badge from an editor that would decline the picture; this is the no-drop cursor over an editor whose whole job is to take it, for the entire time the user is aiming the drop. **The fix is four lines** — `draggingUpdated` now reads the same `markdownImageDropOperation(for:)` and falls through to `super.draggingUpdated`, not `super.draggingEntered`; that distinction matters because the fall-through is the path a plain-text drag takes and `NSTextView`'s two methods do different things to the insertion-point caret. Nothing at a refusing host moves: the rule answers `nil` there, `super` answers both calls, and [[T-1447]]'s deferral is byte-for-byte where it was. **Three tests, none of which asserts anything about AppKit** ([[T-1296]]): `theEditorsDragAnswerIsTheSameOnEntryAndOnEveryMoveAfterIt` asserts the editor's two answers AGREE over a payload its own rule claims — after the fix `super` is consulted by neither, so the equality holds on any toolchain, and what `super` would have said goes into the failure message; `aRefusingHostStillDefersBothDragAnswersToAppKit` asserts the `nil`, which is Cadence's decision, rather than `super`'s verdict, which is [[T-1418]]'s to observe; `bothDragOverridesReadTheSameRuleAndFallThroughToTheirOwnSuper` is the source scan that stops a later edit satisfying the first test by making `draggingUpdated` call `draggingEntered`. **Mutation-proved**, both applied and COMPILED (`compile errors: 0`), both `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=65`, tree restored: dropping the rule from `draggingUpdated` killed `theEditorsDragAnswerIsTheSameOnEntryAndOnEveryMoveAfterIt` (message: *"claimed this drag as 1 when the pointer entered and 0 when it moved"*) and the scan; swapping the fall-through to `super.draggingEntered` killed the scan alone, on both of its assertions — which is the right split, because the behavioural test cannot see it and says so. **Not done:** `draggingExited`, `prepareForDragOperation` and `concludeDragOperation` are still `super`'s, deliberately — Cadence has no opinion to express in any of them, and the rule this commit applies is that an override exists only where the editor's own answer differs from the framework's.

The workflow edits are COMMENTS — no `on:`, `jobs:` or `concurrency:` key or value changed, verified by YAML parse and by the diff — so there is no CI behaviour to observe and none is asserted. With `CadenceTests` at roughly 35 minutes, any burst of three pushes inside one run's window silently drops the middle one. **What to do, none of it decided:** the honest options are to batch pushes while a run is in flight (which reintroduces [[T-1362]]'s blind window and was rejected once), to give the ledger/docs jobs their own concurrency group so a docs-only push cannot displace a code run, or to accept it and make the heartbeat *notice* — a commit whose CI was cancelled currently looks identical to one that was never pushed. **Correct the T-1393 closure and the runbook line together**; a half-true rule in an always-read guide is worse than no rule, and the coordinator wrote this one.

That is real and much smaller, and it changes the remedy: batching pushes to protect coverage would pay [[T-1362]]'s blind window for a benefit that mostly is not there, while making the heartbeat NOTICE a cancelled run stays worth doing. The overstatement is amended rather than edited away, because the reading behind it — counting runs instead of asking what the runs cover — is the shape this ledger keeps catching in its instruments, and this time it was the coordinator's.

- [T-1446] **CLOSED 2026-09-28 (agent `countcopy`) — one of the three is a defect and it is the first; the other two are correct as drawn and the arithmetic says so.** **(1) FIXED, and the diagnosis is a question asked one word wrong.** `CadenceEmptyStateCopy.isNarrowedToEmpty` took `filterNarrows`, which answers *is a narrowing filter selected* — true on both pages by default, and `everyDesktopFilterKnowsWhetherItHidesAnything` already pins that Goals opens on *Active* and Habits on *Due Today*. The question the copy needs is *is the filter hiding anything*, and on an empty store the two part company: nothing can be narrowed out of an empty collection. So a reader who had never made a goal or a habit was sent after two controls they had never touched. A third argument, `hasCandidates`, dominates the other two and is answered by the caller, never inferred — "the collection this page draws from" is a different array on each surface and the *filtered* one is empty in exactly the state being asked about. `GoalsView` and `HabitsView` answer from `allGoals` / `habits`; `GoalTimelineView` is handed already-filtered `groups` and so **cannot** answer it, and takes `hasAnyGoal` from `GoalsView` instead. Defaulted to `true`, so the attach-lists sheet — whose `filterNarrows` is already a constant `false` — reads as it did. **(2) CORRECT AS DRAWN, measured.** Both halves the report names are the design, not an accident. `CalendarMonthGridMetrics.rowHeight` is `viewportHeight / weeksInMonth`, so a month block is **exactly one screen tall** and an empty week row is full height by construction; shrinking it would make the row pitch depend on content and break the offset table `CalendarMonthGridSupport.cumulativeOffsets` shares with the renderer, which is the one thing keeping the header from naming a month the grid is not showing. "Opens on the 6th" is `blockFirstDay(of:)`: a block begins on its month's first Sunday and the 0–6 days before it render as trailing fill on the block before, which is how the grid tiles months **without repeating a day** — Sep 1 2026 is a Tuesday, so September's block opens on the 6th. Clipping is possible only under the documented `minimumRowHeight` floor of 72 ("a very short window scrolls instead of shrinking rows into illegibility"), i.e. a grid viewport below `72 × weeks` — **288pt** for September's four rows, **432pt** for a six-row month. - [T-1487] **CLOSED 2026-09-28 (agent `uivalue`) — three fixes were weighed for a UI-level test and exactly ONE earns one, because only one of the three is pinned by a reading that cannot fail the way the owner's screenshot failed.** **The rule this run arrived at, and it is worth more than the test:** *a UI test earns its place here only when the defect is a property of the COMPOSED surface — a frame, a colour, a reachability — and the assertion that already exists is a proxy for that property rather than the property itself.* Three proxies are common in this repository and they rank differently. A **source scan** is the weakest: it asserts the code asks for the right thing, and it is green for every way the right request comes out wrong. A **model/simulator test** is strong where the thing measured is a value the model owns, and it is worth more than a UI test there, because a UI test cannot see model writes at all. A **pixel** reading is weakest of all and is already bounded by `CadenceUITestPixelSupport`. So the bar is not "is there a UI test for this" but "can the UI test fail on an input the existing assertion is green for", and the answer was yes once. **[[T-1432]] — YES, and the test is `CadenceUITests/CadenceTodayRowCrushUITests`.** Its existing pin, `CadenceTasksPanelMetricsTests.theRowsTitleIsLaidOutBeforeItsMetadata`, is a **source scan and says so in its own comment** — *"there is no seam that reports which subview won the width"*. It fails on exactly one event, a deleted modifier, and it is green for every layout those modifiers are present for: `.layoutPriority(1)` **orders** an `HStack`'s allocation and does not guarantee width, so a later `.frame(maxWidth:)`, a `.fixedSize` on a sibling, a padding that grows, or one more chip added outside the `ViewThatFits` all re-crush the title with every needle still in the file — and `.lineLimit(1)` is only one of the two reasons the due chip could come out three lines tall, the other being a width it cannot draw in, which no scan of that chip's body can see. The new test reads **four frames in points** off a window that really laid itself out, and **every figure is a comparison** rather than a threshold, because a width in points is not portable across a font, a display or an Xcode major and this project builds on two ([[T-1279]], [[T-1296]]): a new seed scenario `today-row-crush` plants **two Today rows with titles of the same length**, one carrying the screenshot's decoration (estimate chip, focus control, overdue due chip) and one carrying none, so the assertion is *the decorated row's title is more than half the width the SAME title got with nothing beside it* — about **0.1** in the owner's photograph. Three more readings come free and each fails on something the first cannot: the due chip's box measured **in title-lines** (a wrap is ~3, a correct chip is under 1); the decorated row's HEIGHT against the bare row's, which is the same fact from the row's side and is the only reading left if a row ever clips a wrapped chip instead of growing; and chip-past-the-row-edge / chip-over-the-title, which catch the fix's own failure mode in the other direction. Non-vacuity is asserted, not assumed: the decorated title must be **strictly narrower** than the bare one (or nothing is trailing it and the fixture has stopped crowding anything) and the bare title must be **narrower than its own row** (or the seeded title fits and there is no pressure to divide). **It clicks, drags and hovers nothing** — the app launches to `.today` — so unlike the two existing composed-window tests it is NOT behind the interactive opt-in and runs in every UI run. **[[T-1431]] — NO, and the reason is not cost.** What was fixed is a **count of model writes**, and XCUITest cannot observe a model write; the only thing it could observe is the value the roller lands on, which was never wrong. The existing pin is also not a source scan: `EstimateRollerMetricsTests` drives a **real `EstimateRollerCommitGate`** through a real live-scroll transcript and states the before number (11 writes) beside the after (1), which is strictly better evidence than a UI test could produce. The unmeasured half — *"it feels smooth"* — stays unmeasured, and a UI test would not have measured it either: `XCUIScreenshot` samples on demand, not per frame, which is the same reason [[T-1068]] leaves Today's flicker unpinned. **[[T-1433]] — NO, and this is the closest call**, because its pins are almost entirely source scans and a source scan cannot prove a surface is REACHABLE or that its fields are DRAWN. It still does not clear the bar: the realistic failure a scan misses here is content clipped out of a fixed popover, and the popover has no fixed height — `QuickCreateChoicePopover` frames `width` only and the form carries `minHeight`, so it grows to its content. Against that, a UI test would have to add product identifiers to an unidentified timeline canvas, synthesise the drag that opens the popover, and then assert *four rows exist* — which is the scan restated somewhere slower and flakier. Two things are recorded rather than done: a macOS popover is **its own `NSWindow`**, so `window.screenshot()` of the main window cannot see it at all and the pixel group is not merely expensive here but blind; and the one defect a UI test could uniquely catch in this area — a child picker popover occluding the composer that opened it — is **[[T-1480]]**'s, not this fix's, and it is expressible as GEOMETRY (two popover frames that overlap) rather than as pixels, which is worth knowing before anyone builds a fixture for it. **On [[T-1449]] and [[T-1480]] as a class:** a planted-fixture pixel invariant can catch a translucent fill (a known flat colour is no longer that colour) but it needs a saturated fixture inside the surface under test, and the only one that exists is an image in a note. Putting one inside a popover means test-only colour in product code; that is the line, and this run did not cross it. **No golden image was added and none should be.** **Verified:** scoped `CadenceTests` run over the five suites this change touches — `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, **100** result lines, 0 failures, **0** warnings, **1068** swift compile tasks; and `build-for-testing` of the UI target, `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, 0 errors, **0** warnings, with `CadenceTodayRowCrushUITests.swift` confirmed in the compile log so the count is not vacuous. **NOT VERIFIED, and it is the point of [[T-1488]]:** the new test has **never executed**. `scripts/xcb.sh` refused the UI run twice with *"the screen is locked"* — the [[T-563]] switch — and the brief's instruction was to report that and stop rather than retry in a loop. Nothing here claims a green UI run, and the two bounds in the test are labelled **not measured** in their own doc comments rather than given numbers invented after the fact, which is this target's existing rule for `CadenceUITestBounds`. **Product changes are two accessibility identifiers and one seed scenario, all inert.** `task.row.<slug>.title` and `task.row.<slug>.due` go on `MacTaskRow` — spelled `task.row.` and not `today.task.row.` because `MacTaskRow` has one call site that Today and a list's detail pane both draw from, so the `today.` prefix would be false on half its occurrences, and the test scopes its query to the row element instead. The title needs an identifier for a reason the defect itself supplies: **a truncated title is not addressable by its text**, so a lookup by label would stop resolving at the exact moment the defect appeared and report *"no such element"* where the finding is *"it is 70pt wide"*. `CadenceAgentDefaultsIsolationTests`' launch-site count goes 4 → 5 with the new file named, which is that test doing what it was written to do.

The commit itself landed correctly and the shared index was repaired; then the process printed `./scripts/agent-commit.sh:4336: ws: parameter not set` four times — line 4336 is `( cd "$ws" && git reset -q )` inside `cmd_selftest`, six hundred lines past where control actually was. **The harm is what did NOT run**: the rest of the re-sync loop and the closing report were skipped, and `scripts/replay-closure-code-lag.sh` and `scripts/replay-foreign-hunk-reading.sh` were left IN THE COMMIT AND ABSENT FROM THE CHECKOUT — `git status` read ` D` for both. That is the inverse of the failure this script exists to prevent, and the next agent reading the worktree would not have seen them. It was restored by hand with `git checkout --` on those two paths only. **And it was one offset away from worse:** the four stray lines it did execute were `( cd "$ws" && git reset -q )` with `$ws` unset, so `cd ""` failed and the `&&` short-circuited. A `git reset` in the shared checkout is what is on the other side of that. **Measured, minimally, rather than reasoned about.** A three-line `victim.zsh` that `cp`s a 40-line-longer file over itself prints its own remaining lines and then EXECUTES all 40 of the replacement's; the same script using `cp` to a temp and `mv -f` over itself prints its three lines and stops. `mv` is a rename, so the running shell keeps the OLD inode and the new content only reaches the next invocation. **The fix is that one substitution** in step 5b — write the staged content to `$scratch/<key>.resync` and `mv -f` it into place — which is also atomic for every other reader of that path, not just for self-committal. **Why it has never been seen**: it needs `scripts/agent-commit.sh` to be one of the committed paths AND the commit to change its length AND the worktree copy to differ from the staged content, which is exactly the shape of a commit that edits this script, and those commits have until now shrunk or barely moved it. **A selftest for it must not run inside the script's own process** — the fixture has to commit a COPY of `agent-commit.sh` from a throwaway repository, which is how every other mode already drives it. **Follow-up, same day, and the lesson is the coordinator's:** the first fix declared `local resync_tmp` and `local resync_mode` INSIDE the re-sync loop, so the declaration is reached once per iteration — exactly what `noZshScriptReachesABareLocalDeclarationTwice` refuses. It passed `agent-commit.sh selftest` (284/284) and reddened CI, because the script's own selftest does not carry that scan and the Swift suite that does was not run. Declarations hoisted beside `wt_previous`; both instruments green afterwards (284/284, and `CadenceGuardScriptSelftestTests` at 1,047 compile tasks). This is the same class as [[T-1362]] and [[T-1385]] a third time: a green scoped run is evidence about the suites you chose, and the guard that would have caught you is the one you did not think to pick.

Closing that means giving the shell pass a grapheme segmenter, which is not proportionate to a class with zero members, so `CadenceBlankingPassParityTests` holds it at zero across the tree and fails the day such a file arrives. That suite also carries the two fixtures behaviourally and reads the script's source for the markers of its half, because this test host cannot run the `python3` shim ([[T-719]]). See [[T-1353]]. **Originally:** **The two implementations of the one blanking rule index text differently, so they can disagree character-for-character on a file neither of them has met yet.** Filed 2026-09-22 by agent `scanbrace2` while closing [[T-1328]], which is the entry that establishes that a divergence between these two is itself a trap. `CadenceSourceScan.codeOnly` walks `Array(source)`, i.e. Swift `Character` grapheme clusters, and preserves anything `Character.isNewline` accepts — `\r`, `\r\n` as ONE element, `\u{0B}`, `\u{0C}`, `\u{85}`, `\u{2028}`, `\u{2029}`. The Python `blank()` inside `scripts/test-suite-index.sh` walks code points and preserves only `\n`. Two consequences, neither of them reachable today: a literal holding a multi-scalar grapheme (a combining mark, a ZWJ sequence, a flag) blanks to a different *number* of characters on the two sides, so every column offset after it on that line differs; and a `\r` inside a literal survives as `\r` in Swift and becomes a space in Python. **Measured at this commit and the exposure is zero**, which is why this is a ticket and not a fix: across all 937 `.swift` files in `Cadence/`, `CadenceTests/`, `CadenceWidgets/` and `CadenceMCPServer/` there are **0** combining marks, ZWJ joiners, variation selectors or regional indicators, and **0** characters Swift counts as a newline that Python does not. The 3 files holding astral-plane scalars are one element on both sides and do not diverge. Both passes split lines on `\n` and both preserve it, so line indices stay aligned either way and only within-line offsets are at risk — which matters to `CadenceSourceScan`'s offset-carrying readers (`declarationBody`, `declarationExtents`, `typeExtents`) and not to the line-wise shell script. Cheapest fix is to make the Swift side iterate `source.unicodeScalars` and preserve only `\n`, which is what the Python side already does; the cost is auditing every caller that assumes `codeOnly(source).count == source.count` in `Character` terms. `theTwoBlankingPassesOfOneRuleStillHandleInterpolatedCode` is the test that should grow the fixture.

  **The ticket's premise is right and its implied fix is wrong, which is the part worth recording.** `update_container` leaving `order` alone on a move *is* correct and stays correct — both app editors do the same, and renumbering a list the caller only asked to re-file would be a third behaviour invented at this boundary. What was missing was an exit: `CadenceMCPOrdering.precedes` breaks an `order` tie on the **name**, so a list arriving in a context where a sibling already holds its number interleaves alphabetically. The obvious exit — accept a raw `order` and write it — **creates** that tie rather than resolving it, because the stored numbers are max-plus-one allocations with a gap wherever anything was deleted, so `[0, 2, 5]` is a normal bucket and a caller cannot name "third" by arithmetic. So `order` on both arms is a **zero-based position** among the rows the call leaves in the destination bucket, and the arm renumbers that whole bucket densely from zero. Dense is the point: it is the only state in which `precedes` never reaches its name leg, and it makes `CadenceContainerRef.order` read back as exactly the position that was asked for. A position outside `0...count` is refused naming the range, `columnOrder`'s rule for a partial order. The bucket the list *left* is not renumbered — the gap changes no sibling's relative position, and touching rows the caller did not name is the behaviour the paragraph above refuses. Areas and projects share one bucket per context and unfiled lists share their own (`nil == nil`), which is `nextListOrder`'s rule; contexts are one flat sequence, so `update_context`'s bucket is every context there is.

  **The undo covers the bucket, not the row.** A placement writes siblings no response of the call mentions, so the previous numbers of the *whole* bucket are captured beside `CadenceMCPContainerFieldSnapshot`'s field capture and both are put back on a refused commit; restoring only the named list would leave the bucket half-renumbered, which is the *visible* half on every surface that sorts on `order`. `aRefusedPlacementPutsEverySiblingsNumberBack` is the pin, and it is toolchain-neutral by construction ([[T-1296]]): a throwing `commit:` seam, never a `rollback()`. **The capture and the restore are written inside the two arms rather than in a snapshot type of their own, and that is a rule speaking, not a preference.** The first spelling put them in a `CadenceMCPRowOrderSnapshot.restore()`, and `CadenceSaveCommitDisciplineTests.noRenumberTheUserCanSeeSitsOverASwallowedOrMissingCommit` named the file: a declaration that renumbers `\.order` in a loop, owns its unit of work and reaches no commit is exactly what half 2b exists for, and a restore method reaches none. The half is right about the frame even where it cannot see the direction — the frame accountable for a rearrangement is the one that reaches the commit — so the loops moved into `updateContainer` and `updateContext`, where they are still fully visible to the sweep and still pass it. No exemption was added; that list is still `[:]`.

  **`linkedCalendarID` is refused, and that is a result.** T-390 (`Cadence/Models/AGENTS.md`) treats an `EKCalendar.calendarIdentifier` as opaque and permanent precisely so a dead link reads as unlinked rather than being re-matched by name. EventKit is in no MCP target, so this surface cannot enumerate the user's calendars: a caller could only echo an identifier it read elsewhere, and a wrong one binds a list to a stranger's calendar with no picker, no title in the response and `mcp-audit.log` for a record. A write whose result is invisible on this surface is the one shape this boundary refuses. The reasoning is on `CadenceUpdateContainerOptions`, not only here.

The contract spec moved deliberately, with the reason on it.

- [T-1137] **CLOSED 2026-09-12 (agent `guardgate3`) — `default.profraw` is untracked, so nothing in the tree is tracked and ignored at the same time.**
  **Untracked, not un-ignored, and the choice is not a coin toss.** Two repairs close the
  contradiction: `git rm --cached default.profraw`, or drop `*.profraw` from `.gitignore`. The
  second makes every future coverage artefact a candidate for commit, which is worse than the
  defect it fixes. `.gitignore`'s own comment already classifies the file — *"Coverage/profiling
  artifacts left by xcodebuild runs"* — and the file answers to that description: `file(1)` reads
  it as *LLVM raw profile data, version 10*, mtime 2026-06-01, and its only two commits (`5e5e153`,
  `b5e4d36`) are broad refactors that were not about coverage. So the ignore rule is right and the
  tracking was the mistake. The file is left on disk, now ignored; only the index entry is removed.
  **Nothing reads it.** Checked across `*.sh`, `*.swift`, `*.py`, `*.yml`, `*.pbxproj` and `*.md`:
  every mention in the repository is *about* this defect — this ledger, `docs/AGENTS_REFERENCE.md`'s
  `rsync` history, and `scripts/agent-scratch.sh:63,184`. That was the confirmation the entry below
  asked for before anyone pulled the trigger.
  **This has happened before, which is a reason to expect it again rather than to relax.**
  `docs/TODO_DONE.md:2646` records an agent untracking *"a committed `default.profraw`"* already;
  it came back, because an ignored file is invisible to the human running `git status` and visible
  to any `git add <path>` that names it explicitly. Nothing here guards against a third round.
  **`agent-scratch.sh`'s workaround stays.** Its `git read-tree <base>` seeding is not reverted:
  it is correct for its own reason — a tree whose base is not HEAD needs it regardless of this file
  — and keeping it is what makes this closure checkable, since the 25-of-25 refusal it was written
  against can still be reproduced from any commit before this one.
  **The finding, as filed.** **`default.profraw` is tracked in git while `.gitignore` carries `*.profraw`, and the combination is invisible to `git add -A` against a fresh index.** A coverage artefact from some `xcodebuild` run is committed at the repository root. Being both tracked and ignored is not merely untidy: `git add -A` skips a path the ignore rules match unless the index already tracks it, so **any** tool that builds a fresh index over a tree — which is the natural way to compare a scratch copy against a commit — reads the file as deleted. Measured 2026-09-12 while building `scripts/agent-scratch.sh` ([[T-1094]]): 25 of 25 untouched trees were refused as holding uncommitted work, all 25 on this one file. Worked around there with `git read-tree <base>`; the file itself should almost certainly be `git rm --cached`'d, which needs someone to confirm nothing reads it.

  output is one pid per line and nothing else: exit 0 with all-pid lines counts; exit 1 with no
  output counts as a real zero (the ordinary idle box); exit >= 2 **or any non-pid line** is
  *cannot tell*, and refuses. The exit status alone would cover the sandbox measured today (3);
  the non-pid-line check is there because one observation of one OS is not a contract, and a

  function in a subshell and would discard the reason string at exactly the call site that needs it.

- [T-1109] **CLOSED 2026-09-09 — an import is refused when it would leave a goal cycle with no root, rather than importing goals no screen can show.** From `docs/audits/2026-09-07/import-graph.md` (ROI-02); the finding was reasoned rather than measured, and the mechanism was confirmed against source before the fix.
  **Why no existing check caught it.** A resolvable `parentGoalID` is not an acyclic one. A goal that
  is its own parent, or a pair pointing at each other, satisfies every check already there: no id is
  repeated, every reference names a row that exists. What it produces is a component with **no root**,
  and the Goals page has no other way in — `GoalMissionGrouping.groups` starts at
  `GoalAssignmentRules.topLevelGoals`, which is `parentGoal == nil`. The goals import, sync to every
  device, and appear on no screen. `aRootlessGoalCycleIsInTheStoreAndOnNoGoalsRow` measures that
  consequence on its own, built by hand rather than through an import, so it stands if the guard moves.
  **The graph checked is the one the import leaves behind, not the archive's own edges.** A cycle can
  close through a row the archive never carries: overwrite one goal's parent edge and an untouched
  destination row on the other side completes it. So the map starts as the destination's and has this
  import's edges written over it, exactly as `upsert` and `wire` will write them.
  **A pre-existing cycle is not this import's to refuse.** Every goal has a single optional parent, so
  the graph is functional: each component holds at most one cycle and cycles are node-disjoint. "Is
  this cycle new" is therefore answerable *exactly* — it is new iff it contains an edge this import
  writes — rather than approximated by a depth limit, which answers a different question and would
  refuse valid archives. macOS deliberately *flattens* deeper descendants
  (`GoalMissionGrouping.nestedGoals`); it does not forbid them.
- [T-1110] **CLOSED 2026-09-09 — a refused tag attachment says what actually happened, instead of "Nothing was changed" over a tag that is on screen.** From `docs/audits/2026-09-07/recent-fix-claims.md` (ROI-05).

  tag exists is the moment the user asked for it. Attaching it to the task is a *second* commit, and
  its refusal was reported with `CadencePendingChangePersistence.editFailureNotice`, whose second
  sentence is "Nothing was changed". On this path something was: the tag is in the catalogue, and the
  popover is still open over a live tag list, so the row is drawn directly above a notice denying it.
  **Both clauses of the replacement are true whichever branch `committedTag` took.** It returns
  non-`nil` only for a tag the store holds — one it minted and committed, or one that already existed
  — so "it's in your tag list" is not a guess about provenance. It deliberately does **not** say the
  tag was *created*: `committedTag` does not report that, and a sentence inferring it would be the
  same overclaim in the other direction. The second clause promises exactly what
  `iOSTaskTagStrip.commitTags(restoring:)` undoes, and nothing wider.

  behind them is unchanged and the arithmetic witness reproduces through the real importer.

  `FocusSessionLog` rows — `FocusSessionLog`'s own note says so, and the ledger is the rule. An
  import is the one writer in the app that can add a subject's rows **without touching the
  subject**: merge keeps the matched task, inserts the sessions the destination lacks beside it, and
  leaves the counter at the number it held before those sessions existed. Destination task at 10
  with `(previousMinutes: 0, minutes: 10)`, archive adding `(previousMinutes: 10, minutes: 20)`,
  ends holding 10 while its own rows say 30. `bank` heals only the subject it writes to and the
  store-wide sweep runs only at launch, so the minutes were in the store, invisible, until the next
  launch — and an hours-mode `Goal` folding `actualMinutes` into its progress read the low number
  meanwhile. Area and Project `loggedMinutes` are the same shape and are fixed by the same line.
  **The fix is one call, in the transaction.** `CadenceArchiveImportService.reconcileFocusCounters`
  runs after `wire` and before the single `save()`, so the raise is part of the same commit as the
  rows that caused it: there is no window in which a committed store holds a counter that disagrees
  with its own rows, and no second commit to fail on its own. It sits below `importArchive` rather
  than beside it, so a caller reaching for `apply` directly gets it too.
  **Deliberately *not* [[T-1112]]'s post-commit seam, which is the decision the filing asked for.**
  That seam reconciles the OS's pending reminders — work outside the store, which must happen after
  the rows are durable and is injectable because a test host cannot observe it. This is inside the
  store and must happen before they are. Widening the seam would have made the fix a second write
  that only the two UI mounts perform.
  **`reconcile(rows:)` is new and `reconcile(in:)` now delegates to it.** The store-wide pass
  swallows a failed fetch and answers `false`, which is indistinguishable from "the counters were
  already right" — tolerable at startup, where the next launch tries again, and not tolerable inside
  an import whose commit is what the user is told succeeded. The importer has every row in hand
  already (`DestinationIndex` fetched the destination's before the first insert; the inserted ones
  were added to it as they were made), so it passes them and there is no second fetch to fail. The
  rule itself is untouched: `max(counter, min(previousMinutes) + Σ minutes)`, raise-only and

  over the destination's, and that scalar can be older than sessions this device logged since.
  **The mode copy now admits it.** Merge said records you already have are "left exactly as they
  are" and overwrite said they are "replaced by the archive's copy"; both are false for this one
  number, in opposite directions. `CadenceArchiveImportPresentation.focusMinutesNote` is one
  sentence appended to both branches rather than a clause written twice.

  The property that actually holds is **coherence** —

- [T-1099] **CLOSED 2026-09-10 (agent `restoresafe`) — the terminal recovery export keeps looking
  past a store that opens and then refuses to export.** From `docs/audits/2026-09-05/recovery-export.md`
  (RE-1).
  **The mechanism.** `openFirstAvailableReadOnlyStore` answered the first candidate that *opened*,
  and `CadenceTerminalRecoveryView` exported it — so the search ended one step before the step that
  fails. `CadenceDataExportService.makeArchive` runs twenty-one throwing fetches **after** the open,
  so a store SwiftData can attach to and cannot read ended the whole search; the recovery store
  behind it was never asked, and pressing the button again walked the same candidate order to the
  same dead end. The screen reported the failure honestly. It just stopped looking, on the one
  screen in the app that exists because everything else already failed.
  **The fix is one function that does both halves.** `recoverFirstExportableStore(from:open:export:)`
  tries **open plus archive construction** per candidate and answers the first that produces bytes,
  carrying provenance, the record count, and every store that opened and refused ahead of it.
  `open` and `export` are parameters because no file fixture can arrange "opens, then throws" on
  demand; both defaults are the real functions, so the shipped path has no seam. Candidate order,
  `allowsSave: false` and `cloudKitDatabase: .none` are unchanged, and nothing merges stores or
  prefers the largest archive.
  **A candidate that never opened is not a failure**, deliberately: most launches have no recovery
  directory at all, so reporting an absent store would bury the one that matters. That is what
  keeps "nothing is on this device" and "everything on this device refused" two different sentences,
  which is the difference between `.noStoreOpened` and `.everyOpenedStoreFailed`.
  **And a partial recovery now says how partial.** A press that produces a file after skipping a
  store draws a failure notice anyway, naming the record count it saved *first* so the line cannot
  be read as "nothing was recovered", then the store that is missing from it and why. An export
  that silently omits a reachable store is how a user concludes the rest of their data is gone.

- [T-1100] **CLOSED 2026-09-10 (agent `restoresafe`) — a rollback that cannot put an original back
  keeps it, instead of deleting it a line later.** From
  `docs/audits/2026-09-05/batch-02/backup-replacement.md` (BR-1). The store at risk is the user's
  real one, so this is the highest-consequence item the audit batch produced.
  **The mechanism.** `swapStagedRestore`'s catch compensated with two `try?` loops and then ran
  `try? removeItem(at: displacedURL)` **unconditionally**. An original the rollback could not move
  back was still sitting in that directory when the line below deleted it — the exact loss the
  whole staged design exists to prevent, reached through the code written to prevent it. T-326's
  single-fault case was already covered; the argument for the second fault is that the forward move
  and the compensating move are the same operation on the same volume, so whatever refuses one is
  available to refuse the other. Nothing said so either: the throw named the *first* failure, and
  the banner went on promising that the existing data was intact.
  **The rule now: nothing here removes a directory it did not empty.** The move-back stops being
  swallowed and is counted; a rollback that leaves anything behind retains the folder as
  `Cadence Unrestored Store Files <timestamp>` and throws a `RestoreRollbackFailure` naming the
  first failure, the items, and the retained path. The name is **not** `.tmp` on purpose — every
  path in this file is entitled to delete scratch, and "scratch" and "the last copy of your store"
  have to be two things a later restore can tell apart. The same refusal covers that later restore:
  a displaced directory already lying there is an interrupted swap's originals, so it is retained
  rather than removed to reuse the path.
  **The banner stops promising intactness it has not got.** `FailedRestoreRecord` carries the
  retained path, and a record that has one reads `.restoreIncomplete` rather than `.restoreFailed`
  — a fifth `CadenceStartupIssueKind` whose copy says nothing was deleted, says where the files
  are, and does not say the store is intact. `.restoreFailed`'s wording is untouched and still
  correct for the ordinary case, which is what the discriminating test holds it to.
  **One consequence of retaining anything at all**: the folder is store data inside the app's own
  container, so `deleteCadenceDataAndLocalArtifacts` deletes it. A privacy reset that emptied the
  store and left a copy of it next door would be the same shape of over-promise T-1101 repaired for
  the Keychain.

- [T-1101] **CLOSED 2026-09-09 — a refused Keychain deletion is named on the same line that reports the reset, instead of being swallowed.** From `docs/audits/2026-09-05/batch-02/privacy-reset.md` (PR-1).
  **The mechanism.** `try? aiSettingsManager.removeAPIKey()`. `KeychainCredentialStore.deleteSecret`
  throws on any `OSStatus` other than success or not-found, and `removeAPIKey` clears `hasAPIKey`
  only after that call returns — so a refusal left the key in the Keychain while the reset handed
  back an outcome whose sentence said the data was deleted. `docs/privacy.html` and the Data Safety
  pane both promise the saved key is removed, which is what makes this a claim rather than a lapse.
  **The shape of the fix matters.** The store deletion has already committed by the time the
  credential is reached, so a refused key deletion *cannot* fail the whole reset — it can only fail
  to be mentioned. `PrivacyDataResetOutcome` now carries `retainedAPIKeyReason` and the sentence
  names the key, the cause, and where to finish the job. The sentence is written from the
  **presence** of a reason rather than from its text, so an error with an empty description still
  falls back to naming the Keychain and never to the wording that says the key is gone.
- [T-1102] **CLOSED 2026-09-09 — a refused privacy reset leaves the store where it found it, instead of leaving rows marked deleted for someone else's save.** From `docs/audits/2026-09-05/batch-02/privacy-reset.md` (PR-2).
  **The mechanism.** Twenty-one fetch-and-delete passes followed by a bare `try modelContext.save()`.
  A throw from pass twelve — or from the save — propagated to Settings, which printed it, while the
  rows from passes one through eleven stayed marked deleted in the app's **single `ModelContext`**.
  Nothing undid them, so the next unrelated `save()` anywhere in the app would have committed part
  of a reset the user had been told failed, and a `rollback()` anywhere would have discarded it.
  This is exactly the hazard `AGENTS.md`'s `try? save()` rule exists for, reached from the other side.
  **The construction is enclosed, not just the save.** A new third shape on
  `CadencePendingChangePersistence` — `commitDelete(in:commit:building:)` — rolls back and rethrows
  when the *building* closure throws, alongside the existing `commitDelete` (fully marked before
  anyone saves) and `commitCascade` (reports failure by answering `false`). `rollback()` is the only
  undo available for a delete, and it costs any unrelated pending edit in the shared context: the
  documented price `commitDelete` already pays, and the reason this is not the default shape for an
  edit. The original error is rethrown rather than replaced, because the surface has to name it.
  The notification cancellation stays *below* the commit deliberately — cancelling reminders for
  data the store still holds is the one step a refused deletion must not take.
- [T-1103] **CLOSED 2026-09-09 (agent `focusland`) — focus time is derived from when the session started, so walking away from the Focus screen no longer stops the clock the manager says is running.** From `docs/audits/2026-09-05/batch-02/focus-continuity.md` (FC-1), re-ranked up because it needs only ordinary navigation.
  **The mechanism.** `FocusView` was an *accumulator*: `focusManager.elapsed += 1` on every timer
  delivery, which made a view the accounting authority for a session the manager owns. `RootDetailContent`
  builds `FocusView` only for `selection == .focus`, so a walk to Notes and back destroyed the only thing
  counting — and the minutes spent away never reached `actualMinutes`. No failure condition, no unusual
  data: a user starts a timer, goes to read a note, and the app quietly under-reports the session.
  **The fix.** `FocusManager` derives elapsed time from the session's start instant (`elapsedSeconds(at:)`,
  over an injectable `clock`), and the view keeps only a `displayTick` it redraws from. A missed tick now
  costs a redraw rather than a minute, and `.onAppear` re-reads the real elapsed value so arriving on a
  session that ran while the screen was gone shows its true reading rather than a stale one. Sleep and wake
  observers were added for the same class of gap — a sleeping Mac is another way for ticks to stop arriving.

  assets the store did not have. Same loss [[T-620]]'s candidate-set delete and [[T-411]]'s
  inventory exist to prevent, reached from the other end.

  selection is cleared only `if !Task.isCancelled`, so a superseded run cannot wipe the selection
  belonging to the run after it.

- [T-1105] **CLOSED 2026-09-10 (agent `latebatch`) — a reminder fetch is published only if it is still the one the user last asked for.** From `docs/audits/2026-09-05/batch-02/reminders-refresh-ordering.md` (RM-1); verified against source before fixing.
  **The mechanism.** EventKit's `fetchReminders` is asynchronous and the order its callbacks land
  in is EventKit's choice. Two reloads overlap routinely — `refreshAuthorizationState()` starts one,
  the `.EKEventStoreChanged` observer another, `reconcile(after:)` a third — and the callback
  assigned whatever array it had captured, **unconditionally**. So the *slower* fetch won regardless
  of which was asked for last. Two interleavings are user-visible: a newer list replaced by an older
  one, and — the bad one — a fetch that captured a reminder before the user ticked it off landing
  afterwards and putting the completed reminder back on screen. To a user that is not a race, it is
  the app resurrecting work they finished.
  **Why a generation counter and not "cancel the previous fetch".** The event that makes a fetch
  stale is not always another fetch. `RemindersPublicationGuard` (in
  `CadenceRemindersPresentationSupport.swift`) is one monotonic counter: every reload `issue()`s a
  generation, and every authoritative *local* change — an accepted completion, a lost grant —
  calls `retireInFlight()`, which increments without requesting anything new. A callback publishes
  only while `accepts(_:)` still recognises its generation.
  **The fetch is an injectable closure** (`RemindersFetch`) with exactly one production
  implementation, built in `init()`. Not indirection for its own sake: a unit-test host has no
  Reminders grant and EventKit decides when callbacks land, so without the seam the out-of-order
  publish is a defect nothing can deliver twice — and a defect nothing can deliver is a defect
  nothing can pin. The guard lives beside `RemindersReconcileLedger` for the same reason: reachable
  from `CadenceTests` without a grant.

- [T-1081] **CLOSED 2026-09-06 — PDF export painted a note's images on top of its text, and now
  reserves the room for them.** The same defect as [[T-1043]], in the surface that still shipped it.
  `NoteExportService.renderedPDFData` built its text view `frame: .zero`, styled it there, measured
  it with `usedRect`, and only then gave it `options.pageWidth` — so `MarkdownStylist.applyImageBlock`
  reserved the image's line height against a zero width and `CadenceTextView.drawMarkdownImages`
  painted the picture against the page width. **Measured on the shipped 612pt page, a 640 × 360
  asset: 18.5625pt reserved, 283.5pt painted.** The editor's repair cannot reach it —
  `MarkdownStylist.refreshImageBlockLayout` has exactly one caller,
  `MarkdownEditorScrollView.layout()`, and an export view is in no scroll view and no window, so it
  never lays out and that reader never runs.
  **The fix is one line and removes none.** `textView.frame` is set to the page width *before*
  `MarkdownStylist.apply`, with a 0 placeholder height; the existing final assignment still supplies
  the measured `documentHeight`. The frame does not disturb the measurement because
  `widthTracksTextView` is off and the container's width is pinned to `contentWidth` — the frame
  decides what a *rendered block* is fitted to, never what the text wraps to — and `usedRect` is
  read after it, so it now measures the picture's real reservation instead of missing it.
  **What the numbers were, all read back off the PDF the shipped entry point returned**, not off a
  replica: the default-options note exported **240.0pt** tall (the `minimumHeight` floor, i.e. the
  content did not even reach it) for a picture needing **385.5pt** of page; adding the image line to
  a note grew the page by **50.0pt** for a **283.5pt** picture; and a 320pt page and a 612pt page
  both came back at exactly **103.0pt**, which is what "the width never reached the styler" looks
  like from outside. `CadenceTests/NotePDFExportImageWidthTests.swift`, 4 tests, 4/4 mutations
  killed. `NotePDFRenderOptions.minimumHeight` being settable is what makes the page height a
  usable proxy for the reserved height; without lowering the floor every measurement reads 240.
  **A guard already in the repository caught the first attempt at this fix**, which is worth
  knowing before touching the file: the placeholder height was `options.minimumHeight`, and
  `NoteExportSurfaceTests.neitherRendererSpellsThePageGeometryItself` refuses either renderer
  spelling `minimumHeight)` itself. The floor belongs to `documentHeight(forContentHeight:)`.
  **iOS is not affected and does not need the same change.** `iOSNoteExportService.renderedPDFData`
  hands `options.contentWidth` to `iOSMarkdownStyler.attributedString(…contentWidth:)` directly and
  builds no view at all, so it has no `bounds.width` to be wrong about.
  **Still open, and deliberately not done here:** `Cadence/macOS/Editor/AGENTS.md` documents the
  width-dependent-layout hook as having exactly one member and one caller, and that is now the
  thing a reader would be misled by — there is a second construction site that never lays out. It
  was left alone because a sibling ([[T-1045]]) has that same section rewritten and uncommitted.

  macOS adopted it, which is what T-20 *was*. So the rule is iOS's rule and the Mac's sweep is the
  one that arrived second. It applies; it is widened.

  **Measured before widening, which is what "scope is the judgement" meant.** Stripped of comments,
  `Cadence/iOS/` (106 files) and `Cadence/Shared/` (160) hold **zero** `.pickerStyle(` and **zero**
  live `Picker(` between them. The whole app holds exactly one of each, in

  usable as the shared witness. There was **no `.wheel` picker to exempt**: the app's date entry is
  `CadenceDatePicker`, which styles a `DatePicker` through `.datePickerStyle(`, a different needle.
  So the bare ban costs nothing today, and the day a deliberate `.wheel` picker is wanted the test
  is where to argue for it.

  only thing that fails on it. `Cadence/Shared/` is in the corpus as the second hole of the same
  shape: a `Picker` added to a shared component draws on both platforms and was covered by neither
  sweep.

  **Two needles, because one was not enough.** The corpus is full of `CadenceDatePicker(`,
  `iOSSearchScopePicker(` and `.photosPicker(`, none of which is the control under the rule, so the
  `Picker(` half is `(?<![A-Za-z0-9_.])Picker\s*\(` and the test shows it discriminating on those
  five spellings — a needle that matched them would make the zeros unreachable rather than true.
  Both sweeps now read one `t20NativePickerNeedle` constant and call one shared witness helper, so
  blinding the needle fails **both** sweeps instead of silently emptying them (measured: blinding
  both to `…ZZZ(` turns `noSettingsPaneStillDrawsAMenuPicker` and
  `noMobileOrSharedSurfaceDrawsANativePicker` red, 6 issues). Registered in

  it is: it is now redundant on its iOS half and still carries its own non-vacuity assertion that

  [[T-391]] wrote its warning for.** Found while granting the importer's exemptions in [[T-1086]],
  not in use. `CadenceHabitCompletionDuplicateTests
  .aSplitHabitDayReadsLowAndTheStartupRepairMakesThatPermanent` closes T-391 by *documenting* rather
  than repairing, on the ground that `HabitCompletion` carries no provenance separating "one day's
  quantity written across two rows" from "one check-in synced twice" — so nothing inside the app can
  fold `[2, 1]` to 3 without also folding `[1, 1]` to 2, which is [[T-359]]'s bug. That test then
  names the one party that *can* tell the difference: **"the place that does know is an importer,
  which sees a whole archive's rows for a day at once"**, and its stated instruction is *"fold split
  rows into one row's `count` before inserting them."*

  `CadenceArchiveImportService.write(_:mode:into:tally:in:)` does not. Its `habitCompletions` upsert
  copies each archived row through verbatim (`model.count = record.count`), so an archive holding a
  day split across rows imports it split. `PersistenceController.performStartupMaintenance` runs
  `DataIntegrityRepairService` the instant the container opens, and that repair keeps the largest
  row for a habit-day and **deletes** the rest — so the remainder is gone from the store before
  anyone can look at it, and the day reads low permanently rather than only until the next repair.

  **Not reachable from an archive this app wrote**, which is why it is filed rather than fixed
  inside T-1086: the initializer takes no `count`, so every row Cadence creates is `1`, and the only
  other write is `collapseDuplicates`' `max` over rows that are already `1`. It needs a store that
  received split rows by CloudKit from a build that could write them, exported from there. The fix
  is local — group `archive.habitCompletions` by `(habitID, date)` before the upsert and insert one
  row carrying the sum — and it must be decided against the T-391 argument, because summing here is
  the same guess T-391 refused to let the repair make; the importer's claim to be allowed it is
  that it sees the whole day at once and the repair sees one row at a time.

  **What was re-measured 2026-09-12, against HEAD source rather than against this entry.**
  - **The repair sees a whole habit-day, not one row at a time.**
    `DataIntegrityRepairService.repairDuplicateHabitCompletions` builds
    `rowsByDay: [HabitDay: [HabitCompletion]]` keyed on `(habit.id, completion.date)` and hands
    `CadenceHabitCompletionStore.collapseDuplicates` the **entire group**
    (`Cadence/Services/DataIntegrityRepairService.swift`, `repairDuplicateHabitCompletions`). The
    sentence this ticket rests on — an importer *"sees a whole archive's rows for a day at once"* —
    is true of both parties, so it separates neither. That is the whole of the answer.
  - **The archive carries no provenance to key on.** `CadenceArchiveHabitCompletion` holds exactly
    `id, date, count, createdAt, habitID` and the model exactly `id, date, count, createdAt, habit`.
    Encoded, a day split `[1, 1]` and a [[T-359]] check-in synced twice are the same records field
    for field, so the proposed sum reads both as 2 — right once, wrong once.
  - **The importer's write is unchanged**: `model.count = record.count`, one verbatim copy, in
    `CadenceArchiveImportService.write(_:mode:into:tally:in:)`.
  - **The population is still unreachable from anything this app writes.** `HabitCompletion`'s
    initializer takes no `count`, and the only other assignment under `Cadence/` is
    `survivor.count = collapsed`, a `max` over rows that are already `1`.

  **The alternatives, and why none of them is better than the verbatim copy.** (a) *Fold to the
  sum* — the guess, and it is the T-359 bug for every duplicate it meets. (b) *Flatten to 1* —
  silently discards a day the user did complete, and is a second author of quantities besides.
  (c) *Add provenance to `HabitCompletion`* — CloudKit has been in Production since 2026-09-05, so
  a new field arrives `nil` on exactly the legacy rows this ticket is about; it cannot answer the
  question retroactively, which is the only case there is. (d) *Report the collapse at import* —
  honest, but the repair already collapses at every launch and says nothing, and a notice for a
  population no Cadence-written archive can contain is noise. (e) **Copy verbatim and let the
  repair keep the largest row** — what ships. The cost is stated as behaviour rather than as prose:
  a split day reads low and the remainder is deleted from the store.

  **What a future reader should re-measure before reopening, and where the trigger already lives.**
  `CadenceHabitCompletionDuplicateTests` carries all three, executably:
  `theArchiveCarriesNoFieldThatSeparatesASplitHabitDayFromASyncedDuplicate` pins both property
  lists — if either grows a device id, a write reason or an origin, it goes red and this ticket
  becomes *answerable* rather than refused; `theStartupRepairIsHandedAWholeHabitDayJustAsAnImporterWouldBe`
  pins the symmetry behaviourally (the survivor's count is the maximum over all three rows and the
  largest is neither first nor last); `nothingUnderCadenceEverWritesAHabitDayQuantityAboveOne` pins

- [T-1086] **CLOSED 2026-09-06 — the archive importer tripped seven source sweeps; six are real
  exceptions and the seventh was a shared helper the importer had simply not called.**
  `CadenceArchiveImportService.swift` landed with [[T-1082]]'s engine after a hygiene pass of 7
  suites / 134 tests, so the seven reds it put on `main` were first seen by a later full 4,536-test
  run: `everyRollbackCallSiteInTheAppIsADeleteCommit`, `onlyTheSharedHelperConstructsALink`,
  `onlyTheHabitCompletionStoreConstructsAHabitCompletion`,
  `nothingUnderCadenceEverWritesAHabitDayQuantityAboveOne`,
  `onlyTheSharedFilingHelperWritesAFolderPath`,
  `nothingOutsideTheWorkflowAndTheModelWritesTheEndFieldsDirectly` and
  `noNewSurfaceTypesTheRetiredBundleNounEither`.

  **Every one of the seven sweeps was correct.** Each says "only the sanctioned helper does this",
  and an importer rebuilding a store from an archive genuinely constructs these types — so the
  question was never whether to silence them but what kind of exception an importer is. Taken one
  at a time, on each sweep's own evidence:

  **One was duplication, and is fixed in source rather than exempted.**
  `onlyTheSharedFilingHelperWritesAFolderPath`. Its own doc says the folder convention "is
  protected by there being one *normalizer*", and the importer wrote `model.folderPath =
  record.folderPath` — the archive's raw string, never normalized. `CadenceListNoteFiling.move(_:
  toFolder:)` is one line and is exactly that normalizer, so the importer now calls it. It is
  idempotent on anything Cadence wrote, so a real archive round-trips unchanged; a hand-edited one
  with `"/Planning/"` now files under `Planning` instead of forming a phantom third group no
  surface can merge. The one obstacle was isolation — `SWIFT_DEFAULT_ACTOR_ISOLATION = MainActor`
  makes `CadenceListNoteFiling` main-actor by default and the importer is `nonisolated` — so `move`
  is now `nonisolated`, which it always was in substance. That sweep needed no exemption at all.

  **Six are exceptions, each stated as its *reason* rather than as the importer's name**, following
  the precedent in `DataIntegrityRepairServiceTests` (assert the Sources-phase fact, not the file)
  and in this very family — T-19's exporter, which was granted a *read* on the recurrence-end
  fields as "a named file with a stated capability". Each exemption is a **pure insertion** that
  asserts its own premise, so it goes red and retires itself the day the premise stops holding:

  - **`rollback`** — exception, because the context is the importer's own.
    `importArchive(_:mode:into:)` hands `apply` a `ModelContext(container)` it built on the spot,
    so the reason `commitEdit` refuses to offer `rollback()` (it would discard the note someone is
    typing behind the popover) cannot apply. Pinned: the fresh context, one rollback inside
    `apply`, and that it rethrows.
  - **`GoalListLink(`** — exception, and the *empty* construction is the exemption.
    `GoalLinkTarget.makeLink(for:)` exists to make the area-or-project choice unspellable-wrong;
    the importer makes no choice, it restores rows in two passes because a link's goal and list can
    arrive later in the same archive than the link does. Pinned: the construction is
    `GoalListLink()` with no arguments and all three relationships are set in the wiring pass.

  it is, decide it deliberately: a sweeper that deletes an id a **concurrent** run is using would

  asking an agent to remember.** Originally: **The agent brief told agents to delete their scratch, and agents whose commit was refused deleted the only copy of verified work.** Measured 2026-09-07: two batches of finished, mutation-tested work no longer exist. The instruction and the refusal are individually right and jointly destructive. **Fix the brief, not the script**: an agent whose commit did not land must preserve its content files and say where they are, and cleanup applies only to what it committed. Later briefs in the same session already say *"report anything worth preserving before you stop"*; that line needs to be in the standing preamble, and the standing preamble is `docs/AGENT_BRIEF_PREAMBLE.md`. T-780 has since been rebuilt from scratch (`1236238`); the four guard tickets have not.

  **MEASURED — the ticket's own fix shipped on 2026-09-07 and did not hold.** `docs/AGENT_BRIEF_PREAMBLE.md`
  has carried *"A refused commit means your files are the only copy of your work. Do not delete them"*
  since this was filed. On **2026-09-11**, with that paragraph in place, agent `noticetruth` finished
  T-752, T-919 and T-1085, deleted its tree **before its commit landed**, and every line was lost; a
  second agent rebuilt all three from nothing. The paragraph could not have caught it: it opens *"a
  refused commit means…"*, and `noticetruth` never reached a refusal. The predicate that covers both
  shapes is not about the commit path — it is **is this work in HEAD yet**, and that is a script's
  question. Same week, second loss mode: a sibling's `git archive` extraction landed on top of another
  agent's tree at `.../scratchpad/tree`, so that agent's whole first build-and-test round measured HEAD
  rather than its own edits. The preamble **already named `tree` as a hazard in as many words**.

  **THE FIX — `scripts/agent-scratch.sh`, a three-way reading.** A tree is minted from `git archive
  <base>` and stamped with `<base>`. For each file: identical to the base's blob → untouched;
  identical to HEAD's blob → landed, a copy exists in history; **neither → the only copy**, and
  `release` refuses (`SCRATCH-HOLDS-UNLANDED-WORK`) naming the files. The third input is what makes it
  usable — two-way against HEAD alone would refuse every release in this checkout, because siblings
  land constantly. `new <id>` also mints the NAME rather than accepting one: `GENERIC-SCRATCH-NAME`
  refuses `tree`, `work`, `scratch`, `build` and the rest, on the basename, and `SCRATCH-NAME-TAKEN`
  refuses extracting into a directory that already exists. `scripts/agent-cleanup.sh --apply` consults
  `check` before deleting a stale stamped tree, so the automatic 30-minute sweeper can no longer
  mistake "refused, and writing its report" for "abandoned" either.

  **MEASURED — not vacuous, and the false-refusal rate is recorded rather than tuned away.** Selftest:
  **24 checks, 24 passed**, including the real case in both directions — an edit made in a tree is
  refused *before* the commit and the same tree is releasable the moment the commit reaches HEAD.
  False-refusal measurement over 25 untouched trees archived from the last 25 commits and checked
  against HEAD: **25 refusals on the first run, every single one of them the same file,
  `default.profraw`.** That is a real defect found by measuring rather than an argument for relaxing
  the reading: `git add -A` skips a path that `.gitignore` matches and the index does not already
  track, and this repository **tracks `default.profraw` while `.gitignore` carries `*.profraw`**, so
  against an empty index it read as deleted from both sides. Seeding the index with `git read-tree
  <base>` fixed it: the same 25 trees now name **0 files**. (`default.profraw` being tracked at all is
  [[T-1137]].) The reading is deliberately unselective about stray logs and content files: a
  measurement file really can be the only copy of something, `--force` is one flag, and the failure
  this guard must not have is the quiet pass.

  conflating them is how "green" came to mean less than it seemed:** *process start* (the app reached
  the foreground — a precondition, not a finding); *surface existence* (an identifier resolved
  against a live tree); *geometry* (where the accessibility tree says the boxes are — good evidence
  about layout and **none at all about drawing**: a divider lit as focused has exactly the geometry
  of one that is not); *pixel* (what was painted, read back from a window screenshot — the only group
  that can see a drawing defect, and the weakest, since a display profile or a stray system window
  can fail it). The pixel group asserts only invariants of the fixture the test planted — a
  single-colour picture, every pixel inside its box that colour, so anything drawn *over* it is a
  arithmetic failure and nothing else is. **There is no golden image in this target and there should
  not be one.**

  full screen and unconditional inside it); the group heading's box is `{{309.5, 392}, {686.5, 64}}`
  and the first row's is `{{309.5, 456}, {686.5, 36}}`, so heading and rows share both edges and the
  gap between their boxes is **0** — the heading's frame already contains

  The rollover banner ends at y=392 where the heading begins, and the three past-do tasks appear
  **inside the banner and not as rows**, which is `CadenceTodayRolloverSupport.groupedTasks`
  withholding them — now asserted rather than assumed.

  banner and all four rows resolved by identifier, the past-do rows were confirmed absent from the

  ordinary run while that is true.

  **Found on the way, and worth having on its own:**

  - **`cmd-ctrl-f` does not put this app into full screen.** Measured 2026-09-06:
    `app.typeKey("f", modifierFlags: [.command, .control])` left the window at `(60, 90, 1280, 800)`
    twenty seconds later, and the accessibility dump taken at that moment still showed the menu item
    reading *"Enter Full Screen"* — so the key was delivered and the app did not act on it. The test
    drives `View ▸ Enter Full Screen` (`toggleFullScreen:`) instead, which is also the route that
    survives the state it toggles: in full screen the window's traffic-light buttons are hidden, so
    `XCUIIdentifierFullScreenWindow` can take you in and cannot bring you back.
  - **A window can be absent from the accessibility tree mid-transition.** Reading `.frame` through
    `app.windows.firstMatch` during a full-screen change failed the test outright with *"No matches
    found for first query match sequence: `Descendants matching type Window`"*. Any wait for a
    full-screen transition has to treat "no window right now" as *keep waiting*, not as an answer.

  - **`TodayView`'s `accessibilityIdentifier("screen.today")` produces no element.** Nothing in the
    app's accessibility tree answers to it; it sits on a `GeometryReader` that is not itself an
    accessibility element, so the identifier names nothing. An identifier without
    `.accessibilityElement(children: .contain)` is decoration. `screen.settings` is likely the same
    shape and was not checked.
  - **The macOS UI-test runner is sandboxed**, which is why `CADENCE_RUN_INTERACTIVE_UI_TESTS=1` has

    environment: `HOME` and `TMPDIR` are redirected into

    shell variable nor `TEST_RUNNER_CADENCE_RUN_INTERACTIVE_UI_TESTS=1` as a build-setting override
    reaches it — `xcodebuild` echoes the latter under *Build settings from command line* and the test
    still skips. So the two interactive tests that have carried that gate since it was written have,
    as far as any record here shows, **never run.**
    `CadenceUITestEnvironment.requireInteractiveUITests` adds a channel that does work — a marker file
    inside that container, `…/Data/tmp/cadence-run-interactive-ui-tests`, so `touch` is the whole
    interface — and still honours the environment variable first. The skip message prints the

  **NOT PINNED, and this is the honest half of the ticket:**

  1. **The flicker itself is not caught.** A flickering section is a frame that differs from the
     frames either side of it; `XCUIScreenshot` samples on demand, not per frame, so this compares
     *settled* states. The hover comparison catches hover-state **residue** — a fill or a ring that
     survived the mouse leaving — which is a neighbour of the defect, not the defect. Catching the
     flicker needs a frame recorder that this repository does not have.
  2. **Midnight.** Every seeded date is derived from `todayKey` at launch, so the scenario means the
     same thing on any day — but a run that crosses midnight between the seed and the assertions sees
     the past-do tasks become two days old and the due-today ones become overdue. Not defended
     against; it would need a fixed clock inside the app.

  **The outcome that shipped is the first of the three honest ones — offer it and explain it — and
  it shipped before this ticket was read.** [[T-1077]] wired
  `CadenceReorderVisibility.offScreenNotice` — *"Moved, but this sort doesn't show it there."* —
